performers: Kerstin Thorborg, contralto; Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam; Carl Schuricht (live; Carl Martin Öhmann sings the tenor songs of the same concert)
intro: Kerstin Thorborg sings “Der Abschied”, the sixth and last movement of Das Lied von der Erde, marked “Schwer”. In the text night falls, a friend is late and a last drink is offered, and between the waiting and the parting the orchestra plays a funeral march.

sections.label: Intro · Low C and solo oboe
sections.mNote: Contrabassoon, horns, harps and tam-tam play the opening

sections.label: A · Alto: the sun behind the mountains
sections.mNote: The alto sings over a held cello note and flute.

sections.label: B · Moonlight, brook and sleeping birds
sections.mNote: Oboe and clarinet figures lead back to the evening scene

sections.label: A′ · Flute and voice, held bass
sections.mNote: The flute returns above the voice and a held bass.

sections.label: C · Harps and mandolin
sections.mNote: Harps and mandolin play before the singer’s lines about the friend.

sections.label: D · Orchestral interlude, Schwer
sections.mNote: Cor anglais and strings begin the long orchestral interlude.

sections.label: A″ · The farewell drink
sections.mNote: The alto’s bare narration returns over low C and tam-tam.

sections.label: E · The friend’s answer, voice veiled
sections.mNote: Strings play softly under his answer and departure for the mountains

sections.label: F · Final section, repeated “ewig”
sections.mNote: Mahler’s own words lead to the repeated final “ewig”.

cues.title: Opening low C, oboe entry
cues.text: A low C sounds in contrabassoon and low strings, with horns, harps and a soft tam-tam stroke. A solo oboe then enters. The marking is Schwer (heavy).
cues.evidence: Universal Edition full score, p. 97: Schwer, low C, contrabassoon, horns, harps, tam-tam, low strings and oboe entry. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/65/IMSLP20582-PMLP47886-Mahler_-_Das_Lied_von_der_Erde_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Source poems by Meng Haoran and Wang Wei
cues.text: Mahler joined two poems. Meng Haoran’s speaker waits for a friend among the mountains, and Wang Wei’s offers a traveller a farewell drink. Mahler knew them through French versions by d’Hervey de Saint-Denys and German poems by Hans Bethge.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives prints the Meng Haoran and Wang Wei poems, d’Hervey de Saint-Denys’s French versions, Bethge’s German and Mahler’s alterations side by side. http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Abschied.htm

cues.title: Date of composition
cues.text: Alma Mahler wrote that the songs were sketched on lonely walks in the summer of 1907. Alfred Roller, who visited that summer, reported: “This summer remained without artistic fruit.” Bethge’s book was announced only on 5 October 1907, and the dated manuscripts indicate that the songs were composed largely in the summer of 1908.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling’s introduction for Universal Edition, March 2010, sets Alma’s memoirs against Roller’s report, the announcement of Bethge’s book in the Börsenblatt on 5 October 1907 and the dated manuscripts: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: Alto recitative, figure 3
cues.text: The alto begins in a narrating tone, without expression (In erzählendem Ton, ohne Ausdruck). The text tells of the sun going down behind the mountains and evening falling over the valleys. A cello holds one long note beneath the voice, and a flute plays a countermelody above it.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 98–99, figure 3: In erzählendem Ton, ohne Ausdruck, held cello and flute countermelody. The tam-tam is silent in this recitative.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The moon as a silver boat
cues.text: The orchestra drops in volume for the line “O sieh! Wie eine Silberbarke schwebt der Mond am blauen Himmelssee herauf”. Translated, it reads: look, the moon floats up like a silver boat on the blue lake of the sky.
cues.evidence: The text as Mahler set it, printed beside Bethge’s version by Mahler Archives: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Abschied.htm . Translation by the site.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Footnotes at figure 9
cues.text: At figure 9 a flute solo accompanies the line about the brook singing through the dark. Mahler added two footnotes on p. 102 of the full score. If the flautist lacks a large enough tone, the oboe takes over, and the alto must not cover the flute solo.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 102, two footnotes at figure 9: the oboe substitutes if the flute lacks a large tone; the alto must not cover the flute solo.

cues.title: Mahler’s changes to Bethge’s text
cues.text: Bethge’s “hardworking people” go home longing for sleep. Mahler changed them to “tired people”, who go home to learn forgotten happiness and youth anew in sleep. At the end of the poem he added a cry of his own, “O Schönheit! O ewigen Liebens — Lebenstrunkne Welt!”
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives prints Bethge’s “Die arbeitsamen Menschen gehn heimwärts” and Bethge’s ending “O kämst du, kämst du, ungetreuer Freund!” beside Mahler’s “Die müden Menschen” and his cry to the world drunk with life: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Abschied.htm

cues.title: Figure 22, flute over double bass
cues.text: After the evening scene, the bare music of narration returns at figure 22, marked “Sehr gleichmäßig. Nicht eilen”. A solo flute plays above a held double-bass note. At “Es wehet kühl”, the singer is in the cool shade of the spruces, waiting for a friend and the last farewell.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 109, figure 22: Sehr gleichmäßig. Nicht eilen, solo flute, held double bass and Es wehet kühl.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Vienna performance, 30 December 1917
cues.text: On 30 December 1917 Willem Mengelberg conducted Das Lied with the Vienna Philharmonic. Its concertmaster Arnold Rosé, who had played it before, told the tenor Jac. Urlus: “Now we have heard Das Lied von der Erde for the first time.” The same day Alma Mahler gave Mengelberg the manuscripts of this song.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s history page for Das Lied von der Erde reports the Vienna performance of 30 December 1917, Rosé’s remark to Urlus (“Jetzt haben wir zum ersten Male das Lied von der Erde gehört”) and Alma’s gift of the manuscripts: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/das-lied-von-der-erde/das-lied-von-der-erde-history/ . Translation by the site.

cues.title: Bruno Walter’s recollection of Mahler
cues.text: Bruno Walter recalled that Mahler showed him the score of this movement, pointed to one passage and asked: “Can you think of a way of conducting that? Because I can’t.” The voice and solo instruments run across the barlines, and the passage is marked Ohne Rücksicht auf das Tempo (without regard for the tempo).
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s page on Lied 6 gives Walter’s account and the direction Ohne Rücksicht auf das Tempo: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/das-lied-von-der-erde/das-lied-von-der-erde-lied-6-der-abschied/ . Wikipedia’s article on the work footnotes the anecdote to Henry-Louis de La Grange, Gustav Mahler, vol. IV: A New Life Cut Short (Oxford University Press, 2008), p. 510: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das_Lied_von_der_Erde

cues.title: Orchestral interlude, funeral march
cues.text: After the singer’s cry to a world drunk with life, the orchestra plays alone. Cor anglais and strings return to the opening figures. From them a heavy funeral march develops, with pizzicato basses, harp and tam-tam.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 116–117, figures 35–38: end of the first poem, Mäßig and Schwer. Christian Utz identifies the funeral march as bars 288–373: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recorded durations of the Abschied
cues.text: Conductors take this march at different speeds. Colin Davis’s 1981 Abschied lasts nearly thirty-five minutes; it is the slowest in Christian Utz’s survey of ninety-two recordings and fills 51 per cent of the whole cycle, against 43 per cent in Klemperer’s 1951 recording. Schuricht’s lasts twenty-eight minutes fifty-two.
cues.evidence: Christian Utz, Musicologica Austriaca (2018): Davis’s Abschied is the slowest of the recordings compared, with 50.9 per cent of the cycle against 43.4 per cent for Klemperer in 1951, and the funeral march is bars 288–373: https://musau.org/parts/neue-article-page/view/37 . The Internet Archive transfer of this performance runs 1,732 seconds: https://archive.org/details/06-das-lied-von-der-erde-mahler-concertgebouw-amsterdam-carl-schuricht-5.-x.-193

cues.title: Recitative, bars 374–380
cues.text: The alto returns to plain narration. A friend dismounts and offers the farewell drink, then asks where the traveller is going and why. Low cellos and basses hold C beneath her, and the tam-tam sounds.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 127, figure 48: erzählend und ohne Espressivo, low C in cellos and basses, and tam-tam. Utz identifies this recitative as bars 374–380.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Interruption from the audience
cues.text: Just before this passage, at about 19:30, a woman in the hall shouted. The person who uploaded the recording heard “Deutschland muss raus … Herr Schuricht”, or perhaps “Deutschland über alles”. The concert took place five weeks into the Second World War and seven months before Germany invaded the Netherlands.
cues.evidence: The Internet Archive item description for this concert, with the clip isolated as a separate track, gives the time, the uploader’s hearing of the words and the date of the invasion, 10 May 1940: https://archive.org/details/06-das-lied-von-der-erde-mahler-concertgebouw-amsterdam-carl-schuricht-5.-x.-193

cues.title: The traveller’s reply
cues.text: The traveller replies with a veiled voice (“seine Stimme war umflort”). Fortune has been unkind to him, and he is going into the mountains for rest. The strings play pianississimo near the fingerboard, and the voice is marked sehr weich und ausdrucksvoll.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 129–132: seine Stimme war umflort, pianississimo strings marked Griffbrett, and sehr weich und ausdrucksvoll in the voice. The complete text is printed by Mahler Archives.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Wang Wei’s “Farewell”
cues.text: In Wang Wei’s poem the traveller says he is “at odds with the world” and goes home to rest by the South Hill. “Please go. Ask no more. Endless, the white clouds.” Bethge kept the clouds (“ewig, ewig”), and Mahler’s ending replaces them.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives prints Wang Wei’s “Farewell” in translation, d’Hervey’s French, Bethge’s ending (“Und ewig, ewig sind die weissen Wolken”) and Mahler’s altered text: http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Abschied.htm

cues.title: Mahler’s added ending to Bethge
cues.text: Bethge’s traveller ends among eternal white clouds. Mahler wrote a new ending, which Stephen E. Hefling identifies as beginning “Still ist mein Herz”. In it the heart waits for its hour, the earth flowers in spring and grows green again, and the far horizons shine blue for ever.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives compares the endings. Stephen E. Hefling identifies Mahler’s own lines as beginning Still ist mein Herz: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: First performance, Munich, 1911
cues.text: Bruno Walter conducted the première in Munich on 20 November 1911, six months after Mahler’s death. Mahler had avoided numbering the work for fear of a Ninth. He gave it its title on the same sheet on which he gave the number 9 to the symphony he had just completed.
cues.evidence: The Berlin Philharmonic’s programme note by Tobias Bleek gives the première of 20 November 1911 in Munich under Walter and the six months since Mahler’s death: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/gustav-mahler-das-lied-von-der-erde/ . Stephen E. Hefling’s Universal Edition introduction describes the superstitious reluctance to number it and the sheet with the title and the number 9: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538

cues.title: Mengelberg’s conducting score
cues.text: A note on the title page of Willem Mengelberg’s score records that Mahler thought this his most difficult work to perform. On the last page Mengelberg wrote “soft, softer, pianississimo” several times as a reminder to himself.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s history page for Das Lied von der Erde describes Mengelberg’s score, its title-page note and the reminder on the last page: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/das-lied-von-der-erde/das-lied-von-der-erde-history/

cues.title: Repetitions of “ewig” and close
cues.text: “Ewig” — for ever — is sung again and again. Harps, mandolin and celesta play short notes against held wind and string chords. The last sung syllables fall from E to D, and the final C-major harmony keeps an A within it.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 138–146, repeated ewig and closing scoring. Printed p. 146 shows the final vocal E–D, added A in the C-major harmony, and the mandolin falling silent before the final held chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Cello C after the fermata rests
transitions.from: Intro · Low C and solo oboe
transitions.to: A · Alto: the sun behind the mountains
transitions.how: The introduction ends in rests held by fermatas. At Fließend. Im Takt, a cello holds a long C and the alto enters. Around the voice, the flute plays a countermelody.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 98, figure 3: fermata rests, held cello C, alto and flute.

transitions.title: Return of the opening bass tread
transitions.from: A · Alto: the sun behind the mountains
transitions.to: B · Moonlight, brook and sleeping birds
transitions.how: The flute’s phrase and the held cello note fade under fermatas. At figure 4, marked Tempo I, the contrabassoon and harps play the opening bass tread again. No tam-tam is written here. Trilled clarinet chords, the oboe’s curling line and horn entries follow and lead into the moonlit scene.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 99, figure 4. The return uses contrabassoon and harps; no tam-tam is written here.

transitions.title: The flute above a held bass
transitions.from: B · Moonlight, brook and sleeping birds
transitions.to: A′ · Flute and voice, held bass
transitions.how: The words about the sleeping world lead into a long stillness, with a held double-bass note underneath. At Sehr gleichmäßig. Nicht eilen, the alto resumes the bare narration and the flute returns with its curling melody. In the full score this join falls on pp. 108–109, at figures 20–22. It ends the evening scene and restarts the recitative.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 108–109, figures 20–22, ending the evening scene and restarting the recitative.

transitions.title: Mandolin and harps follow the held note
transitions.from: A′ · Flute and voice, held bass
transitions.how: The flute descends and the bass note fades under a fermata. At Fließend the mandolin and two harps enter with a new flowing accompaniment. The second violins take up the short repeated figure and the first violins enter with a longer melody. The conductor moves step by step towards beating whole bars, marked “Allmählich zu ganzen Takten übergehend” at figures 23–24 (full score, pp. 109–110).
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 109–110, figures 23–24: mandolin, harps and Allmählich zu ganzen Takten übergehend.

transitions.title: The cor anglais continues alone
transitions.how: The alto’s final phrase ends over held winds and strings. At Mäßig, the cor anglais takes up the curling figure over short violin notes. Bassoon, horns and harps follow. The orchestral passage leads into Schwer and the funeral march, with pizzicato low strings.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 116–117, figures 35–38, from the end of the first poem to the funeral march.

transitions.title: From the march to the low-C recitative
transitions.how: The march thins out into held chords and short phrases in the wind. The harps play their last notes sharply. At figure 48 the cellos and basses hold a low C with quiet tam-tam strokes, and the alto begins the recitative about the farewell drink (bars 374–380).
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 126–127, figure 48; Utz, section 4, identifies the low-C recitative at bars 374–380.

transitions.title: Pianississimo strings after the fermata
transitions.to: E · The friend’s answer, voice veiled
transitions.how: Woodwinds and harps interrupt the narrator with echoes of the march. Her phrase about the friend’s veiled voice ends beneath a fermata. The strings enter pianississimo, then bow near the fingerboard (Griffbrett), and flute and horn phrases surround the friend’s soft reply.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 128–130, figure 51: fermata, pianississimo strings, Griffbrett and the answering vocal phrase.

transitions.title: Harps enter at Langsam
transitions.from: E · The friend’s answer, voice veiled
transitions.how: The strings slow through Ritenuto molto and then hold their notes under a fermata. At Langsam, two harps begin ppp arpeggios. Over sustained violins and pizzicato lower strings, the alto sings of the earth blossoming again. Mahler marked the passage Ohne Steigerung, without any increase in force.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 134–135, figures 57–58: Riten. molto, Langsam, PPP, Ohne Steigerung, harp arpeggios and vocal entry.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, VI. Der Abschied, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: Printed pp. 97–146. The first two recitatives pair flute with a held low string note; the third adds tam-tam and omits flute. Mandolin joins the harps in the waiting scene and the closing pages.

timeline.note: The oboe enters above low C, horns, tam-tam and harps.
Strings enter quietly with the oboe and horn phrases in C minor.
The alto sings above a held note in the cellos and a winding melody in the flute.
Contrabassoon and harps play the opening figure again beneath clarinet trills and oboe.
The alto describes the moon’s silver boat among quiet winds, harps and strings.
A solo flute plays the brook’s melody beside the alto, who sings very quietly.
Brass and harp glissandos swell beneath the words about the breathing earth.
The strings and brass play a crescendo under the voice’s long phrases.
Small woodwind figures accompany the birds settling in their branches.
The flute returns above the alto and a long double-bass note.
Mandolin and harps begin the flowing accompaniment; the strings take up its repeated figure.
The orchestra moves forward with the singer’s question to the absent friend.
Harp and mandolin accompany the singer’s walk with a lute.
The alto and strings rise towards the first poem’s final cry.
The singer rests; cor anglais and strings begin the long orchestral interlude.
The march resumes at A tempo subito after a held pause.
Brass hold a pedal note beneath violins playing on the G string.
The alto narrates above low C in cellos and basses, with tam-tam strokes.
Woodwinds and harps interrupt the narration with fragments of the march.
The strings play pianississimo, bowing near the fingerboard, beneath the friend’s voice.
Flute and quiet strings accompany the traveller’s words about going home.
Harps and quiet strings accompany Mahler’s lines about the greening earth.
Harps and celesta sound among sustained wind chords and string notes.
The alto repeats ewig among quiet winds, strings, harps and celesta.
Flute, oboe, trombones and strings hold the last chord after the voice stops.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Kerstin Thorborg (contralto), Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam (orchestra), Carl Schuricht (conductor)
fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The item does not say which score edition the orchestra used or whether any passage was cut. The first edition (Universal Edition, 1912) is the score read for the notes on this page; the 1939 performing materials may differ.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The date is in the item’s title and date field and agrees with the Carl Schuricht article; the Mahler Foundation gives only “October 1939 broadcast concert, live”. It is not the upload date (the item was added on 2 July 2022).

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Named in the item title (“Concertgebouw Amsterdam”) and in the Mahler Foundation’s listing of a live Amsterdam concert; “Concertgebouw” names both the orchestra and the hall, and neither source names a room.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The item names no label and does not state the medium it was copied from. The Mahler Foundation’s discography records a Bel Age CD made “from acetates” of the broadcast; whether this file derives from that issue is not stated.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: No catalogue number is given for the source of this file.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No acetate matrix, side or take numbers appear in the sources consulted; this is not a claim that they cannot be recovered.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item names an uploader account but no transfer or restoration engineer; an uploader is not automatically a transfer engineer.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item’s added and public dates (2 July 2022) are upload dates, not transfer dates.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Internet Archive derivatives of a WAV original: this file is a variable-bit-rate MP3 (170 kbps); FLAC and spectrogram derivatives of the same WAV are also listed.
fields.note: The item description calls it “a good recording”. It does not describe noise reduction, speed correction or equalisation. The Internet Archive item also carries a separate 15-second clip (track 07, “Zwischenruf 6. Satz at 19 min 30 sec (3x)”) in which the uploader isolated an audience interjection that he places at about 19 min 30 s of this movement; the clip is not part of this recording and the words shouted are the uploader’s uncertain hearing.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor, and that career would pay for everything else.
